To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a diet eliminating artificial colours and benzoates in 3 year olds is associated with a reduction in hyperactivity, as reported by parents, that this effect is reversible by challenge and that this effect is not influenced by the level of hyperactivity or atopy in the children.

the ingestion of artificial food colourings (and the preservative sodium benzoate) is associated with behavioural changes, and that these effects are more marked in children with hyperactive behaviour.

1) the effects of food additives are not limited to children with hyperactivity; 2) the effect of additives is not limited to children who have atopy; and 3) the effect of food additives on children’s behaviour is detectable by parental report but not by the use of a simple objective assessment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of artificial food colourings, and a preservative (benzoate) on behaviour in a general population group of preschool children.
the possible effects of artificial food colourings on the behaviour of young children.
the possible effects of food additives on the behaviour of children in the general community.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of artificial food colourings on behaviour have been shown to be present in 3 year old preschoolers, and are detectable by parents.

there is no evidence to support the view that the ingestion of artificial food colourings or benzoate preservatves by 3 year old hyperactive children is a causal factor in their hyperactive behaviour.

there is a general adverse behavioural effect in 3 year old general population children from artificial colours and benzoates, but that this does not affect the subgroup with hyperactivity or atopy more than others.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a general adverse affect on behaviour in 3 year old preschool children of artificial food colourings, which is detectable on parental ratings.
artificial food colouring in combination with benzoate preservers may be a cause of hyperactive behaviour in a significant number of children in the population.
there are effects of artificial colourings and preservatives on behaviour but that these are not restricted to those with a diagnosis of hyperactivity or atopy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are no subgroups that are more vulnerable to the adverse effects of artificial colourings and preservatives.

food additives have an adverse effect on children’s behaviour, and that this effect is not limited to children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder or those with allergies, but is a more general phenomenon.
the effects of artificial colours and preservatives on children’s behaviour are not confined to children with attention deficit disorder or atopy.
